# FDG8016

> DO NOT use `IEnumerator<T>`, `IEnumerator`, or any other type that implements either of these interfaces, except as the return type of a `GetEnumerator` method.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 8.3 Collections.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG8016
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application warning, test none
- Status: verified

Message: Do not use the enumerator type '{0}' in the signature of '{1}'

Test profile: test classes are public only for the test framework; their signatures are not API. FDG8016 reports a type that is or implements IEnumerator (so IEnumerator&lt;T> too) as the type of a parameter, a return value or the result of a returned Task&lt;T> or ValueTask&lt;T>, a property or indexer, or a field of an externally visible member. The return value of a method named GetEnumerator is not reported, as the text allows. Overrides and interface implementations are not reported. Uses as a type argument are not seen, so coverage is partial. Changing the type changes the public signature, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

> **Anthony Moore:** I’ve seen a lot of violations of this guideline ever since LINQ has been available. The review body made an explicit decision that LINQ should not change this guideline. Your callers can end up with a clumsy object model if they choose not to use LINQ or use a language that does not support it.

Types returning enumerators from methods other than `GetEnumerator` cannot be used with the `foreach` statement.
